newsitem.title: USA: U.S. domestic politics lurk behind Mideast summit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. domestic politics lurk behind Mideast summit.

text.p: Despite the insistence of White House officials that President Bill Clinton's emergency Middle East summit had nothing to do with U.S. politics, the November election loomed over each development.

With a new crisis between Israelis and Palestinians threatening to unravel U.S.-led Mideast peace efforts, Clinton was forced to host the emergency summit that brought Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to the White House, along with Jordan's King Hussein.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher defended the summit, saying: "We thought the situation was sufficiently urgent, sufficiently grave, that the risk of violence and chaos was sufficient to justify the president's intervention."
Before the two-day summit began, administration officials went out of their way to lower expections -- and in the end they came up with little to boast of.
Clinton on Wednesday admitted he had little to announce at the close of the summit, aside from the fact the parties had agreed to continue to talk, but he nonetheless cast it as a victory.
"This is a risky business," Clinton said of his efforts, as the other participants sat mute in the East Room, declining to make any public statements in that setting.
"I think I've made that clear, and I'll do my best to be there every step of the way," he said.
The risks of Clinton's efforts clearly spilled into the domestic political arena as well -- although his aides tried to create an imaginary separation.
"This isn't about politics," a White House official said defensively on Tuesday night, following the first day of tense talks. "Nothing to do with it."

He was visibly annoyed when stopped in a White House hallway by a reporter and asked about the summit and its implications for the Nov. 5 presidential election. Clinton holds a substanial lead over Republican rival Bob Dole in virtually all public opinion polls.

As the senior official walked away, he joined a small group of other administration strategists who were walking from the West Wing of the White House to the private residence -- to join Clinton for a campaign strategy session.
Although Clinton publicly was talking about world peace, privately he was piecing together a strategy to keep him in the White House for four more years.
An increasingly frustrated Dole, whose political message has been swept aside in the tidal wave of attention on the summit, turned to bemoaning what he called Clinton's "photo op" diplomacy.
Dole planned to meet with Netanyahu on Wednesday night, after the conclusion of the summit. He had no plans, however, to meet with Arafat or King Hussein, the other key participants.
Dole has gone out of his way to be supportive of Israel -- issuing a statement flatly declaring that "our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order."

Ironically, most opinion polls of Jewish-American voters find the majority of them support Clinton -- whose administration has tried to nurture and build on the peace efforts pushed by Republican President George Bush.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich quickly chided Clinton's "photo-op press conference ... where nothing was accomplished."
"It is very unfortunate to see this kind of lack of thought, lack of structure ... this kind of lack of planning and lack of systematic leadership," Gingrich said.

Christina Martin, a Dole campaign spokeswoman, declined immediate comment on the results of the summit. The Republican challenger and his aides are in a difficult position when it comes to high-profile foreign affairs -- forced to walk a tightrope.
Too much criticism of Clinton can backfire, while too much silence can only help him appear presidential.
Dole must now hope to recapture lost ground on Sunday night, when he and Clinton square off in Hartford, Conn., for the first of two televised presidential debates.
